ADHD Medications

stimulants · atomoxetine · alpha-2 agonistsStimulant or not, and what do you monitor?

1Script2Urgent3Differential4Workup5Criteria6Severity7Treatment8Follow-upPractice
1Drug script
Bottom line
  • Age 6 or older: a stimulant first; under 6: behavioral therapy (parent training) first
  • Before a stimulant: cardiac history and exam, plus BP, HR, height and weight; consider an ECG (electrocardiogram) if cardiac disease, an abnormal exam or sudden cardiac death in the family
  • Misuse or diversion: atomoxetine. Mania on a stimulant: taper or stop it. Guanfacine or clonidine: taper, never an abrupt stop
What it is

Drugs for attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD): stimulants first; atomoxetine, guanfacine and clonidine as nonstimulant alternatives

Mechanism

Stimulants dopamine is the main target; amphetamines also push catecholamines out of storage vesicles

Atomoxetine blocks the norepinephrine transporter; spares the nucleus accumbens, so no addiction risk

Guanfacine, clonidine alpha-2 agonists that cut norepinephrine release

Drugs

Stimulants: methylphenidate; amphetamine salts, dextroamphetamine and lisdexamfetamine

Nonstimulants: atomoxetine; guanfacine and clonidine

Also used for

Narcolepsy (second line, after modafinil); methylphenidate may be considered for severe depression with a short life expectancy

Binge eating disorder: lisdexamfetamine

Insights

On a prescribed stimulant, tolerance and withdrawal alone are not a use disorder

Lisdexamfetamine is a prodrug activated in the gut, so it can also be used with a drug-misuse history; atomoxetine stays first when misuse or diversion is the concern

Adverse effects, by drugtap to open
StimulantsAppetite and weight loss, insomnia, headache, stomachache, How muchOn average, HR rises 5 to 10/min and systolic BP 4 to 6 mm HgHeight growth slows over about 2 years of use; tics can emerge; rarely mania or psychosis
AtomoxetineNausea, sedation, irritabilityRare liver injury; suicidal ideation in children and teens
Alpha-2 agonistsSleepiness, low BP, slow pulseRebound hypertension and a fast pulse after an abrupt stop
2Urgent risks
ManiaA manic or psychotic episode on a stimulant; known bipolar disorder raises the risk Psychosis riskNew psychosis in about 1 in 660 adolescents and young adults on a stimulant; amphetamine carries about twice the risk of methylphenidate

If a manic episode begins on a stimulant, choose taper or stop the stimulant and treat the mania first.

Liver injuryOn atomoxetine: itching, dark urine, jaundice, right upper quadrant tenderness

If jaundice or laboratory evidence of liver injury appears, choose stop atomoxetine and never restart it.

Suicidal thinkingAtomoxetine raises suicidal ideation in children and teens; watch most closely in the first months and after dose changes
Abrupt stopGuanfacine or clonidine stopped suddenly: rebound hypertension (persistent, at times with encephalopathy, on guanfacine extended-release)

If an alpha-2 agonist is to be stopped, choose a taper, no faster than 1 mg every 3 to 7 days for guanfacine.

3Differential
Which effect is it, most tempting first
EffectFingerprintDecides it
Days of little sleep, grandiosity and rapid speech in a child with ADHDEpisodic; ADHD is chronic
Agitation, paranoia, fast pulseDilated pupils; pills taken beyond the prescription, or a family member's
New blinking, sniffing or grunting after a stimulant startsTics can emerge on a stimulant; they do not rule one out
Physiologic dependenceTolerance, or a crash when a prescribed dose is missedSupervised, prescribed use: not a use disorder
4Workup
Clues that change the answer
CluePoints toNext move
Classmates buying his pills, or a family member taking themDiversionSwitch to atomoxetine
Past mania or psychosisA stimulant can tip a bipolar patient into maniaPrescribe a stimulant only with caution
Doses often missedRebound hypertension on an alpha-2 agonistChoose a drug other than guanfacine or clonidine
Pause point
Preschooler, hyperactive and impulsive at home and at preschool Offered as clonidine or guanfacine, or diphenhydramine to calm him Under 6, behavioral therapy comes first, with or without a diagnosis → Parent training in behavior management
Teenage girl once on methylphenidate, now arguing about rules; schoolwork fine Offered as restarting methylphenidate No inattention, hyperactivity or impulsivity: the defiance is chosen and normal for her age → Educate the parents about adolescent development
7Treatment
1

1st lineUnder 6

Behavioral therapy: parent training in behavior management

Medication if the response to behavioral therapy is inadequate or symptoms are moderate to severe

2

1st lineAge 6 or older

A stimulant (methylphenidate or an amphetamine), with behavioral therapy
3

Misuse riskMisuse or diversion is a concern

Atomoxetine
4

2nd lineStimulant fails or is not tolerated

Atomoxetine, guanfacine or clonidine

Less effective than stimulants

5

AdultsAdult ADHD

A stimulant, as in children

Alpha-2 agonists have limited adult data

Manage by effect
EffectDo
Appetite and weight lossGive the dose after a meal; follow weight on growth charts
Slowed growth in heightPlot height on the growth chart throughout treatment In practice:Medication holidays on weekends, holidays or school breaks may be tried
Continue with close monitoring; tics do not rule out a stimulant
Rising BP or HRRecheck off and on the drug
8Follow-up
Monitoring
  1. Before startingCardiac history and exam; BP, HR, height, weight
  2. Throughout treatmentBP, HR, growth, sleep, appetite, tics
  3. Atomoxetine, early monthsSuicidal thoughts; liver symptoms
WhenCheckWhy
Before any ADHD drugCardiac history and exam; BP, HR, height, weightStimulants raise HR and BP; baseline for growth
Throughout stimulant treatmentBP, HR, height, weight, sleep, appetite, ticsGrowth in height can slow
Atomoxetine, first months and dose changesSuicidal thoughts, unusual behavior; liver symptomsSuicidal ideation in youth; rare liver injury
Guanfacine or clonidineBP, HR, sleepinessLow BP, slow pulse; rebound if stopped abruptly
Interactions
WithEffectDo
Serious, sometimes fatal reactions: high fever, rigidity, unstable vital signsNo stimulant or atomoxetine until 14 days after the MAOI stops
Fluoxetine or paroxetine, with atomoxetineAtomoxetine exposure up 6- to 8-fold because these drugs block cytochrome P450 2D6 (CYP2D6)Raise atomoxetine more slowly, every 4 weeks
Practice
  1. 9-year-old boy with ADHD; his parents agree to start a stimulant inattention and impulsivity at home and school for 2 years his uncle died suddenly while running at age 28 HR 88/min · BP 104/66 mm Hg · normal heart sounds → Electrocardiogram → sudden cardiac death in the family is a reason to consider an ECG before a stimulant, even with a normal exam
  2. 4-year-old boy brought by his mother for his behavior at home runs off in stores, climbs furniture, interrupts constantly same reports from his preschool teacher for 8 months no injuries; development otherwise normal → Parent training in behavior management → under age 6, behavioral therapy (parent training) comes first; medication is considered if the response is inadequate or symptoms are moderate to severe
  3. 16-year-old boy with ADHD returns after his methylphenidate ran out early his mother found classmates paying him for pills grades slipping; symptoms clearly impair him HR 76/min · BP 118/72 mm Hg → Atomoxetine → a diverted stimulant calls for a nonstimulant: atomoxetine has no addiction risk
  4. 34-year-old woman with ADHD and depression asks to start an ADHD drug stopped phenelzine, taken for depression, 5 days ago takes no other medications HR 72/min · BP 116/74 mm Hg → Wait until 14 days after the last phenelzine dose → stimulants and atomoxetine are contraindicated within 14 days of stopping an MAOI (monoamine oxidase inhibitor)
  5. 11-year-old girl on atomoxetine for 3 months for ADHD 4 days of itching, dark urine and fatigue yellow sclerae; tender right upper quadrant ALT 640 U/L · AST 520 U/L · T 37.0 °C → Stop atomoxetine and do not restart it → jaundice or laboratory evidence of liver injury on atomoxetine: stop it and never restart
  6. 12-year-old boy with ADHD has a headache and feels jittery took guanfacine every day for a year; ran out 3 days ago no stimulant; no new drugs BP 148/96 mm Hg · HR 112/min · pupils normal → Rebound hypertension from stopping guanfacine → guanfacine stopped abruptly brings rebound hypertension and a fast pulse; it is tapered instead
  7. 15-year-old girl with ADHD, on amphetamine for 2 years 6 days of sleeping 2 hours a night without fatigue talks rapidly; plans to start three businesses urine drug screen negative · HR 90/min → Stop the amphetamine and treat the mania → a distinct episode with little need for sleep is mania, not ADHD; the stimulant is tapered or stopped and the mania treated first

Eating Disorders covers lisdexamfetamine for binge eating.
Substance Intoxication and Withdrawal covers stimulant intoxication and misuse.
SNRIs, Atypical Antidepressants and MAOIs covers the MAOI washout.
Transferable rule

Before an ADHD drug, check the heart, the growth chart and the risk of misuse; misuse calls for atomoxetine, and an alpha-2 agonist is tapered, never stopped abruptly.
